definitions.definition: A Latin phrase meaning 'the end of the self' — the point where a system hits its own limits and cannot save or fix itself.
definitions.example: Like a video game character that can't heal itself because its own healing power is broken.

definitions.definition: When different ideas or proofs from separate fields all point to the same conclusion.
definitions.example: Like five different detectives solving the same crime without talking to each other.

definitions.definition: A proven rule that says if a math system is consistent (has no contradictions), it cannot prove its own consistency using only its own rules.
definitions.example: Like a person who can't prove they're honest just by saying 'I'm honest' — they need evidence from outside themselves.

definitions.definition: A set of rules and statements that never leads to a contradiction.
definitions.example: A game where the rules never say you both win and lose at the same time.

definitions.definition: Basic starting assumptions that are accepted as true without proof.
definitions.example: Like saying 'all right angles are equal' in geometry — you just start there.

definitions.definition: A step of reasoning that goes from one fact to another.
definitions.example: If you see wet grass, you infer it rained.

definitions.definition: Trying to prove yourself correct using only your own ideas or rules.
definitions.example: Like a student grading their own test and saying they got an A — it's not trustworthy.

definitions.definition: A proven rule that says no language can define its own concept of 'truth' without creating a paradox.
definitions.example: Like trying to write a dictionary that defines every word, including the word 'definition' — you get stuck in a loop.

definitions.definition: A way to say 'this statement is true' inside a language.
definitions.example: In English, the phrase 'is true' is a truth predicate.

definitions.definition: A statement that seems to contradict itself, like 'this sentence is false'.
definitions.example: If you say 'I always lie', and you're telling the truth, then you're lying — it's a paradox.

definitions.definition: The classic paradox: 'This sentence is false.' If it's true, it's false; if it's false, it's true.
definitions.example: Like a sign that says 'Ignore this sign' — you can't follow it without breaking it.

definitions.definition: Something outside a system that you use to check if the system is correct.
definitions.example: Using a ruler from the store to check if your homemade ruler is accurate.

definitions.definition: A proven rule that says no computer program can always figure out whether another program will stop or run forever.
definitions.example: Like trying to write a program that can predict if any other program will crash — it's impossible to do perfectly.

definitions.definition: A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem.
definitions.example: A recipe for baking a cake is an algorithm.

definitions.definition: Something that no computer, no matter how powerful, can ever do.
definitions.example: A computer can't solve the halting problem for all programs — it's computationally impossible.

definitions.definition: A physical law that says in a closed system, disorder (entropy) always increases or stays the same — it never decreases on its own.
definitions.example: Your room gets messier over time unless you clean it — that's the second law in action.

definitions.definition: A system that doesn't exchange energy or matter with anything outside it.
definitions.example: A sealed thermos of coffee is a closed system — no heat or coffee gets in or out.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system.
definitions.example: A scrambled egg has higher entropy than an unbroken egg — it's more disordered.

definitions.definition: A rule that says erasing one bit of information always releases a tiny amount of heat — information processing has a physical cost.
definitions.example: Every time you delete a file on your computer, a tiny bit of heat is produced — that's Landauer's principle.

definitions.definition: The smallest unit of information, either a 0 or a 1.
definitions.example: A light switch that is either on or off stores one bit of information.

definitions.definition: A minimum amount of energy that must be spent — you can't make it cheaper no matter how clever you are.
definitions.example: Like the minimum price of a candy bar — you can't pay less than that, even if you bargain.

definitions.definition: Related to heat, energy, and how they move or change.
definitions.example: A car engine's efficiency is a thermodynamic question — how much heat turns into motion.

definitions.definition: Able to keep itself going without help from outside.
definitions.example: A plant that gets all its energy from sunlight is self-sustaining — it doesn't need food.

definitions.definition: A price that can't be undone — once paid, you can't get it back.
definitions.example: Burning a log releases heat that can't be put back into the log — that's an irreversible cost.

definitions.definition: The fact that things stay organized and don't fall apart immediately.
definitions.example: Your phone doesn't suddenly turn into dust — that's persistence of order.

definitions.definition: Information that makes sense and fits together without contradictions.
definitions.example: A clear instruction manual has coherent information; a jumble of random words does not.

definitions.definition: An endless chain where each thing depends on the next, with no starting point.
definitions.example: Like saying 'I need a friend to help me, but that friend needs a friend, and that friend needs a friend...' forever.

definitions.definition: A foundation or base that supports everything above it.
definitions.example: The concrete foundation of a house is the grounding layer for the walls and roof.

definitions.definition: Something that is accepted as true with no explanation — 'it just is'.
definitions.example: Saying 'the universe exists because it does' is treating it as a brute fact.

definitions.definition: The idea that everything must have a reason or cause for being the way it is.
definitions.example: If a ball rolls, there must be a reason — someone pushed it or gravity pulled it.

definitions.definition: An idea that can't be proven wrong, no matter what evidence you find.
definitions.example: Saying 'invisible unicorns exist' is unfalsifiable — you can't prove they don't.

definitions.definition: Something that is its own foundation — it doesn't need anything else to support it.
definitions.example: Like a building that holds itself up without any ground — impossible in real life, but this is a philosophical idea.

definitions.definition: Something that must exist and cannot not exist.
definitions.example: A triangle must have three sides — that's necessary. A chair could be missing a leg — that's not necessary.

definitions.definition: Something that exists because of itself, not because something else made it.
definitions.example: A rock exists because of natural processes; a self-existent thing would exist without any cause.

definitions.definition: A theological term meaning 'self-existence' — God exists from himself, not from anything else.
definitions.example: In theology, God has aseity — he doesn't need anyone to create him.

definitions.definition: The idea that God is not made of parts — he is one simple, undivided being.
definitions.example: Unlike a car that has many parts, God is simple — no pieces to take apart.

definitions.definition: The quality of being eternal — without beginning or end.
definitions.example: A circle has no start or end point — that's like eternality.

definitions.definition: The ultimate foundation that everything else depends on for existence.
definitions.example: In some religions, God is the ground of all being — everything exists because of him.

definitions.definition: The traditional qualities that many religions assign to God, like being all-powerful, all-knowing, and eternal.
definitions.example: Omnipotence (all-powerful) is one of the classical attributes of God.
